title: A Master of Both Chan and the Pure Land: Master Hanshan
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Surveying the whole life and conduct of Master Hanshan, like Master Yongming (the Sixth Patriarch of the Pure Land school) and Master Chewu (the Twelfth Patriarch of the Pure Land school), his cultivation and propagation of both Chan and Pure Land were brilliant and celebrated, and he is listed in the Record of Sages of the Pure Land; thus he is both a Chan-lineage master and a Pure Land-lineage master. inline.s: Surveying the entire course of Master Hanshan's life, he resembled Master Yongming (the Sixth Patriarch of the Pure Land school) and Master Chewu (the Twelfth Patriarch of the Pure Land school) in that his practice and his propagation of both Chan and Pure Land were outstanding and shining, and his name is recorded in the Record of Sages of the Pure Land; thus he is both a Chan-lineage master and a Pure Land-lineage master. Only because Master Hanshan's body is enshrined side by side with the body of Master Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch of the Chan school, at Caoxi is he mistakenly taken merely for a Chan patriarch. In truth, Master Hanshan, in order to enable students of Buddhism to be free of birth and death in this very life, pointed everywhere back to the Pure Land; all his life he advocated and spread the Pure Land practice, perfect in both principle and fact; and moreover he set an example himself, seeking rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and won brilliant success. He is beyond doubt a patriarch of the Pure Land school.
The Record of Sages of the Pure Land states:
Ming dynasty
Deqing
; a holy monk of the Ming era)

Deqing, style name Chengyin, in later life known as the Old Man Hanshan, was a son of the Cai family of Jinling. His mother dreamed that Avalokiteshvara brought a boy and gave him to her, and so she conceived. When he was born
(he was born in the twenty-fifth year of the Jiajing era of the Ming Shizong emperor)
, he was wrapped in a white double membrane
(a white double-layered membrane)

. At the age of nineteen he left home and gave himself single-mindedly to Buddha-recitation. One night in a dream he saw Amitabha Buddha manifest before him, standing in the sky where the sun sets; his face, eyes, light and marks were all perfectly clear. From this time on, the radiant sacred form
(from this time the luminous sacred form of Amitabha Buddha)
was ever before his eyes. Presently
(before long)
he went to Mount Wutai to practice concentration and discovered what was originally possessed
(he fully awakened to mind-nature)

. He pricked himself to write the Avatamsaka Sutra in blood, and with every stroke of the brush he recited one name of the Buddha. After a long time, whether in movement or stillness, he was one with the practice.

Full understanding of the original possession: Concerning the matter of Master Hanshan's complete awakening to mind-nature at thirty, the Record of the Autobiographical Chronological Account of the Old Man Hanshan in the Collection of Dream Wanderings relates: “I lived alone here (Longmen on the North Terrace of Mount Wutai), holding up a single thought; when people came I did not speak, only looked at them. After a long time I looked upon men as tree stumps, until I reached a state where I did not know a single character. At first, because a great wind often arose and howled through a thousand hollows, and the melted ice in the mountain streams rushed and thundered like a torrent, in the quiet I heard sounds like an army of thousands of horses and men setting out, and I found it very disturbing. So I asked Master Miao (Master Miaofeng), and the Master said: ‘The realm arises from the mind, not from outside. I have heard the ancients say: for thirty years hear the sound of water without turning the sense of mind, and you will realize the perfect penetration of Avalokiteshvara.’ On the stream there was a single-log bridge, and every day I sat or stood on it. At first the sound of water was quite distinct; after a long time, when a thought stirred I heard it, and when no thought stirred I did not. One day, sitting on the bridge, I suddenly forgot my body, and then the sound was utterly still; from then on all the sounds were hushed and no longer troubled me. Each day I ate wheat bran mixed with wild vegetables, and took them with a drink of cooked rice (one gō of rice). At first people sent me three dǒu of rice (ten gō make one shēng, ten shēng make one dǒu), and after half a year there was still some left. One day, when I had finished the porridge and was walking, I suddenly stood still; I saw neither body nor mind, only a single great treasury of light, perfect, full, and utterly still, like a great round mirror, in which mountains, rivers and the great earth appeared as reflections. When I came out of it, all was clear and luminous; I searched for body and mind and could not find them at all. Then I spoke a verse: ‘In a flash the frantic thought is stilled, within and without the bases and dusts are all pierced through; turning over and breaking into the great void, the myriad forms arise and vanish.’ From then on, within and without were perfectly still, no longer hindered by sound, color, and marks; the doubts and graspings of former times were that very moment quite dissolved. When I looked at the cooking pot (the pot for cooking rice), it had already grown dusty; because I was alone without a companion, I did not know how long a time had passed.”

One in movement and stillness: When Master Hanshan was thirty-two, he resolved to pierce himself and write with blood-ground gold (piercing himself to draw blood and mixing it with gold dust to write the sutra) a single copy of the Great Square, Broad and Complete Buddha Avatamsaka Sutra. When Empress Dowager Li learned of this, she bestowed gold and paper for Master Hanshan to write the sutra. In April of the following year Master Hanshan began to write it. While copying, no matter whether the dot or stroke was large or small, with every fall of the brush his mind recited one name of the Buddha. When some monks and laypeople came touring the mountains and reached the Master's quiet room, they would often exchange greetings and ask for instruction, and the Master would respond and converse while his hand never ceased its copying. Some of these were eminent old friends, and the Master would invite them to sit upon the meditation seat and discuss the Dharma with them, while all the while his hand went on writing the sutra. The Master did so every day; though people came and went and he received and spoke with them, his writing of the sutra did not cease, and in his mind no mark of movement was to be found. Many old scholars (elderly, senior scholars) who heard of the Master's condition could hardly believe it. One day the old scholars led a crowd of disciples to the Master's quiet room, wishing to verify what it was all about. They deliberately questioned and made a clamor beside the Master and disturbed him in every sort of way; when the Master finished a section, they took it and compared it with the original, and it truly had not the slightest error. Only then were they convinced that the Master's accomplishment was no ordinary thing. But they still did not understand it, and asked Master Miaofeng: “Why can Master Hanshan use one mind for many purposes?” Master Miaofeng replied: “My elder Dharma-brother's samadhi of Buddha-recitation has reached its utmost purity!” (See the Collection of Dream Wanderings
Record of the Autobiographical Chronological Account of the Old Man Hanshan)
In the twenty-third year of the Wanli era
(the twenty-third year of the Wanli era of the Ming Shenzong emperor, when Master Hanshan was fifty)
, he dwelt quietly at Mount Lao
(he withdrew to the Naluoyan grotto of Mount Lao by the Eastern Sea)
, and Empress Dowager Li ordered that gold be sent to build a monastery there
(the Empress Dowager Li sent gold and silver to have Master Hanshan build a monastery there)
, bestowing the plaque name Haiyin. At the time, the Empress Dowager repeatedly sent eunuch envoys
(envoys sent from within the palace, mostly eunuchs)
to repair various stupas and monasteries. Those in power at court who were at odds with the eunuch envoys
(who harbored a grudge)
had the Dongchang
(the Dongchang, a Ming-dynasty secret police agency whose matters could be reported directly to the emperor, and whose power exceeded that of the Embroidered Uniform Guard)
dispatch runners
(harassing agents)
disguised as Daoist priests
at the time the emperor
Ming Shenzong
revered Daoism
to strike the drum of petition
(the drum suspended outside the court, which allowed subjects to sound it so their case would be heard, whether to remonstrate or to seek redress)
, reporting the matter as embezzlement. The matter implicated Deqing
(the matter implicated Master Hanshan; Qing, that is Deqing — Master Hanshan)
, and he was convicted of
(found guilty of)
privately building a monastery, and exiled to garrison Leizhou
(sent into exile at Leizhou to serve in frontier garrison duty; Leizhou is the prefecture on the Leizhou Peninsula in the southwest of Guangdong province)
. Wherever Deqing went he preached the Dharma in cap and robes
(because his monastic registration had been revoked by the authorities, he preached wearing the cap and robes of a Confucian scholar)
, and further made the vow to spread the great sutras, composing commentaries on the Lankavatara and Shurangama and other sutras.

The matter implicated Deqing: The affair implicated Deqing (Master Hanshan). At that time Empress Dowager Li believed devoutly in Buddhism and performed many Buddhist works, while the Shenzong emperor, because he believed in Daoism, had long detested the eunuchs who were constantly going about on Buddhist business. Once, when the Empress Dowager sent a eunuch envoy to Mount Lao in the Eastern Sea, the inner court angered Shenzong over some incident, and the Empress Dowager was also drawn in. This gave the powerful courtiers opposed to the Empress Dowager just the opening they wanted; they planned first to remove the eunuch envoy who had delivered the sutras, and then to use the old rumor of the magicians' disturbance to strike at the Empress Dowager. So they had the Dongchang dispatch runners, disguised as Daoist priests, to ascend the hall, strike the drum, and present a bill falsely accusing Master Hanshan of embezzling the national treasury silver. The emperor read it and could not but fly into a rage, and issued an edict to arrest the Master and the envoy who had delivered the sutras.
In the forty-second year
(the forty-second year of the Wanli era of the Ming Shenzong emperor, when Master Hanshan was sixty-nine)
, by a gracious edict he resumed the monk's robe
(he resumed the monastic robe)
. On his way back he passed by Mount Lu, and built a hermitage beneath Wuru Peak, following the practice of Master Yuan
(Master Huiyuan)
of marking out the six periods of the day
(taking recitation of the Buddha through the six periods as his fixed practice; the six periods are equivalent to twelve hours of our time)
, and his cultivation of the Pure Land karma grew ever more refined.
At that time a Chan practitioner of Haiyang asked to receive the precepts, and took the occasion to ask the essentials of cultivating the Pure Land. Deqing
(Master Hanshan)
said:

The Buddha said that the methods of practice for escaping birth and death are many in their skillful means, and only the recitation of the Buddha's name in seeking rebirth in the Pure Land is the most direct and essential. This practice the Buddha himself proclaimed without being asked; it equally covers the three capacities and gathers in all four assemblies; it is not a provisional expedient
(a provisional measure)
set up for those of lower faculties.

The sutra says: If you would purify the Buddha land, you must first purify your own mind. Now, to cultivate the Pure Land karma, one must take a pure mind as the root. To purify one's own mind, the first thing is to keep the precept-root pure. For the three of the body
(killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct)
, the four of the mouth
(false speech, idle talk, harsh speech, and divisive speech)
, and the three of the mind
(greed, anger, and ignorance)
— these ten evil karmas are the cause of suffering in the three evil paths. Now the essential of upholding the precepts is first that the three karmas
(bodily karma, verbal karma, and mental karma)
be pure, and then the mind is of itself pure. Within this pure mind, wearying of the suffering of Saha, make the vow to be reborn in Amitabha's land
(that is, the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)
, and establish the proper practice of reciting the Buddha's name.

Yet in reciting the Buddha's name one must be deeply in earnest about birth and death: first cut off outward entanglements, take up the single thought alone, and take the one phrase “Amitabha Buddha” as the very root of life, never forgetting it in any thought, never breaking it in any mind. Throughout the six periods of the day, whether walking, standing, sitting, lying, taking up the spoon or raising the chopsticks, turning and bowing, in activity or stillness, in leisure or busied, at all times, without dullness and without confusion, and with no extraneous condition
(the mind not reaching out and clinging to other matters)

Using the mind in this way, after a long time it becomes wholly ripe and familiar, until even in dreams it is never lost, and waking and sleeping are one; then the effort grows fine and dense, and is beaten into a single mass — this is the time when one gains strength. If one recites until the single mind is not scattered, then at the end of life the realm of the Pure Land appears before one, and one is naturally not detained by birth and death but moves Amitabha Buddha to release light and receive and guide one away — this is the sure token of rebirth. Yet single-minded recitation of the Name is indeed the proper practice.

Moreover one must supplement it with visualization, and it becomes even more sure and esoteric. The Buddha spoke the sixteen subtle contemplations for Queen Vaidehi, and through them one can accomplish the matter within a single lifetime. Now among the sixteen contemplations
(the sixteen kinds of visualization set forth in the Sutra of the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life spoken by the Buddha)

, choose whichever suits you. Either contemplate alone the fine marks of the Buddha and the bodhisattvas, or contemplate the realms of the Pure Land — such as the lotus flowers and precious ponds described in the Amitabha Sutra — contemplating as you wish. If the visualization becomes distinct, then throughout the six periods of the day the Pure Land appears right before you, and at the end of life, in a single instant
(in a single instant, one is suddenly reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)

. Using the mind in this way, upholding the precepts with care, forever cutting off evil thoughts and afflictions; with this pure mind, keeping visualization and recitation joined without interruption — the true cause of the Pure Land is nothing beyond this.
There was again a layman of pure mind who asked: My recitation of the Buddha's name cannot become a single mass; I beg you to instruct me. Deqing instructed him, saying:

In cultivation, the first thing is to be deeply in earnest about birth and death. If the mind is not earnest about birth and death, how can the recitation of the Buddha's name become a single mass? Moreover, for immeasurable kalpas sentient beings have given rise to false thoughts in every thought, their affection-root firmly shut and covered. Even in this life, when you wish to cultivate and transcend the world
(even if in this very life you wish to cultivate and leave the world)
, has there ever been a single thought in deep earnest over birth and death? In the ordinary course of the day, thought after thought follows the affections
(ordinarily thought after thought flows along with the consciousness-based affections)

, and you have never examined yourself. Now you wish, with a shallow and floating faith, to cut off the birth and death of many kalpas — this is what is called “a cup of water against the fire of a cartload of firewood.” How can there be such a principle?
(how could there be such a principle?)
If one is truly in earnest about birth and death, so that in every thought it is like saving one's head from burning
(burning)

, then one fears only that having lost this human body, it is hard to regain it in a hundred kalpas. You must grip firmly this one sound of the Buddha, determined to overcome your false thoughts. In every place, thought after thought present before you
(every thought is the Buddha-thought come before you)

, not veiled by false thinking. Practicing with bitter, earnest effort in this way, after a long time it becomes wholly ripe, and you naturally respond; without seeking a single mass, it forms itself into a single mass.
This matter wholly requires your own exertion. If you only make Buddha-recitation a matter of outer show
(merely putting on a display)
, then even in the year of the donkey you will have no benefit
(so to the year of the donkey there is no time of benefit — that is, so you will never have any benefit)
. You must be resolute and brave, and never hesitate.
[Like a head on fire]: a description of a grave matter that admits no delay and overrides everything else.
He dwelt at Mount Lu for several years, then went
(arrived at)

to Caoxi. In the tenth month of the third year of the Tianqi era he showed a slight illness. He said to people: “This old monk's worldly conditions are nearly at an end.” He bathed, burned incense, sat upright
(sat straight and composed)
and passed away, with a light that illumined the sky
(a light shone and filled the whole sky)
, at the age of seventy-eight.
A light that illumined the sky: In the Collection of Dream Wanderings, a disciple records the scene at the time, saying:
(the tenth month of the third year of the Tianqi era)
on the eleventh day, at the si hour
(nine o'clock in the morning)
, he took leave of Lord Zhang
(Master Hanshan took leave of Governor Zhang of Shaoyang, who had entered the mountains to pay his respects)
. At the shen hour
(three o'clock in the afternoon)

he drank water, bathed, burned incense, and told the assembly: “Great assembly, you should bear in mind that the matter of birth and death is great and that impermanence is swift.” He sat upright with one mind and passed away. At that time a hundred birds cried mournfully, and the four assemblies wailed without ceasing. Through the starry night a fine light illumined the sky, and those across the mountains all suspected that the temple had caught fire
(all suspected that the temple had caught fire)
. Three days later
(three days after his passing)
, his countenance was as in life, his hair had grown
(zhǎng, the hair had continued to grow)
, his lips were red, there was a slight sweat at the tip of his nose, and his hands and feet were like silk.”
Master Hanshan, in the Collection of Dream Wanderings,
in the “Preface to the Ultimate Words of Master Yunqi,” says:

As for the single practice of the Pure Land — cultivating the samadhi of Buddha-recitation — it is that which comprehensively gathers in the three capacities, wholly encompasses the sudden and the gradual, and is accomplished within a single lifetime; there is nothing that surpasses it.”
Here Master Hanshan clearly points out that the Pure Land practice is the ultimate teaching — “nothing surpasses it” — the most perfect and complete method. I now excerpt this text below:

[The three faculties] The strength of sentient beings' good roots is of three kinds: high, middling, and low. [Sudden and gradual] The sudden teaching and the gradual teaching. The sudden teaching is the teaching that brings swift and immediate attainment; the gradual teaching is the teaching that brings attainment through gradual progression.

As for the single practice of the Pure Land — cultivating the samadhi of Buddha-recitation — it comprehensively gathers in the three capacities, wholly encompasses the sudden and the gradual, and is accomplished within a single lifetime; there is nothing that surpasses it. The Buddhas and patriarchs of old have urged it with all their might, and have done so more than once. But alas, later students, aiming at emptiness and mystery, consider Chan the highest and belittle the Pure Land so that they will not practice it. Now that we are in the Dharma-ending age, and sentient beings are heavy with defilement, how can everyone claim to be of the high faculty? Many deceive themselves, never measuring their own spiritual capacity, but merely echo others in empty agreement and never make a real effort — is this not self-deception? Alas! The Chan school has for a long time lacked a clear-eyed good teacher
(the Chan school has long lacked a clear-eyed good teacher)
, and no one corrects this bias
(thus no one comes to correct this deviation)
. As for those given to doctrinal learning
(study of the teachings and doctrines)
, they busy themselves with empty and shallow talk, most of it contrary to reality
(mostly contrary to reality)
; not only do they have no Chan, but the teaching-eye is not clear — and never worse than today.
Master Yunqi
(that is, Master Lianchi)
, early
(in ancient usage the same as “early”)

awakened to mind-only, and therefore vigorously advocated the Pure Land to remedy the ills of the Dharma-ending age. He established a monastery himself, taught his disciples by his own example, and never for a day or night intermitted, for nearly
(almost)
forty years. For this reason, throughout the land monks and laypeople
(clergy and laity)
trusted and followed him in great numbers. The Master's commentary the Shuchao on the Amitabha Sutra expounded the matter exhaustively
(made a complete and thorough elucidation of the purport of the Pure Land)

. As for his ordinary instruction, he mostly raised mind-only to illuminate the meaning of the Pure Land. Mr. Zhu, the layman of Empty Mind, was his inner-room disciple; these words recorded by him he entitled “The Ultimate Words.” Truly it is the perfect mirror of the Chan school, the compass of the one mind, and the golden probe that directly picks away the film from the eyes of the Dharma-ending age

(it is precisely the golden probe that restores sight to the blind eyes of sentient beings in the Dharma-ending age. [Golden probe] an instrument for scraping the film from the surface of the eyeball and restoring sight to the blind)
In the Collection of Dream Wanderings
in the “Ritual Manual for Transmigration,” Master Hanshan again said:
This
(rebirth in the nine grades)

— though one has not yet cut off afflictions, because once one is born in that land, sees the Buddha and hears the Dharma, and dwells in the stage of non-retrogression, one will never again fall into the birth and death of the three realms. From there one makes the vow to return to the three realms to save living beings, and so one comes and goes freely, no longer detained by the afflictions of birth and death. Therefore Master Yongming said: once you see Amitabha, what need to worry that you will not awaken? This is exactly so. This single practice can be accomplished within one lifetime of sincere, earnest effort; once one is born there, one suddenly escapes birth and death and forever leaves the cycle. Such a direct practice — why should one fear not to cultivate it, and even despise it? Yet to awaken through Chan investigation of the matter of birth and death is hard, while to settle birth and death through Buddha-recitation is easy — it only requires that the person have a single thought of true earnestness and bitter effort. From ancient times, those born in the Pure Land are countless and numberless; all these worldly people see with their own eyes yet do not believe — what then can be believed? I now exhort the wise of high intelligence to trust their own mind, and not to wrongly believe in false doctrines. Even within this practice, there are very many who cultivate both Chan and the Pure Land, as Master Yongming said: recite the Buddha and investigate Chan; investigate Chan and recite the Buddha. That is the so-called “having Chan and having the Pure Land, like a tiger with horns: in this present life a teacher of people, in the future a Buddha and patriarch.” This too is the highest practice.
Master Hanshan left home at nineteen, shaving his head and taking ordination, and at once gave himself to reciting the Buddha's name. In his Autobiographical Chronological Account the Master writes:
So I gave myself single-mindedly to Buddha-recitation, day and night without ceasing. Before long
(after reciting in this way not long)
, one night in a dream I saw Amitabha Buddha manifest, standing in the sky where the sun sets. I saw his face, eyes, light and marks, all perfectly distinct. I received his feet and touched my head
(I knelt and with both hands received the two feet of Amitabha Buddha, touching them with my head)
, with boundless grief and longing. I further wished to see the two great bodhisattvas Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta
(and wished to see the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara and Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta)
, and they at once appeared in half their forms
(the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara and Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta then appeared in half their forms)
. From this time the Three Sages were ever radiantly before my eyes
(from this time the Three Sages, luminous and bright, were ever before my eyes)
, and I was confident that my cultivation could be accomplished
(and so I believed that my own practice could bring the fruit of attainment)
[The Three Sages] The Three Sages of the West: Amitabha Buddha, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, and the Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta.

blocks.text: 3. Attaining the Way at Mount Wutai

inline.s: When Master Hanshan was thirty he attained the Way at Mount Wutai. In his Autobiographical Chronological Account the Master writes:
One day, when the porridge was finished, as I was walking, I suddenly stood still
(suddenly stood and entered concentration)

; I saw neither body nor mind, only a single great treasury of light, perfect, full, and utterly still, like a great round mirror, in which mountains, rivers and the great earth appeared as reflections. When I came out of it
(emerging from concentration)
, all was luminous
(all was a single expanse of light)

; I searched for body and mind and could not find them at all. Then I spoke a verse: “In a flash the frantic thought is stilled, within and without the bases and dusts are all pierced through; turning over and breaking into the great void, the myriad forms arise and vanish.” From then on within and without were perfectly still, no longer hindered by sound, color, and marks, and the doubts and graspings of former times were that very moment dissolved. When I looked at the cooking pot, it had already grown dusty; because I was alone without a companion, I did not know how long a time had passed
(returning to the room, I saw that a thick dust had grown on the cooking pot; because I lived alone without a companion and no one asked the time, I did not know how long it had been)

Master Hanshan vigorously spread the Pure Land throughout his life. Master Ouyi, the Ninth Patriarch of the Pure Land school, when instructing that the Pure Land is the practice for transcending birth and death, said:

Moreover, in the degenerate age those who teach the Dharma falsely are as many as the sands of the Ganges; the blind lead the blind, and they pull one another into a pit of fire. Therefore Master Yongming said: “With no Chan but with the Pure Land, of ten thousand who cultivate, ten thousand go.” “With Chan but without the Pure Land, of ten people nine take the wrong road.” And the Master Han of ours said: “At present, if one has Chan and no Pure Land — it is not merely that nine in ten go wrong, I would venture to guarantee that eleven do.” These are all words of deep compassion and great mercy, true words and real words. I humbly beg: all you good people, do not fall into wild conceit and self-deception; you must earnestly reflect on impermanence, believe, vow, and recite the Buddha, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. If this body is not saved within this lifetime, in what other life will it be saved?”
(General Discourse at the Renyi Monastery, Fengnan, Shexi)
Master Ouyi himself also held Master Hanshan in the highest esteem. In the autobiography he wrote in his later years, Master Ouyi wrote:

At twenty-three ... I resolved to leave home and investigate the great matter. At twenty-four I dreamed of bowing to Master Hanshan, weeping that my affinity was so slight and that we had met too late. ... In the course of a month I dreamed three times of Master Han. The Master had gone to Caoxi, and I could not follow him afar. So I shaved my head under the teacher Xueling, who gave me the name Zhixu. Master Xue was a disciple of the Old Man Han.”
At the same time, Master Hanshan and Master Lianchi, the Eighth Patriarch of the Pure Land school, shared a deep Lotus-bond of friendship. Master Hanshan, in the Collection of Dream Wanderings
in his Autobiographical Chronological Account, says:
In the fourth year
(the fourth year of the Wanli era)

bingzi, when I was thirty-one. In the third spring month, Master Lianchi visited on his tour of Mount Wutai and stayed a number of days; of an evening we sat together conversing, and our minds were in deep accord.”
In the forty-fifth year, dingsi, when I was seventy-two. In the first spring month I went down from Shuangjing to mourn at Yunqi
(for Master Lianchi)

. At the time more than a thousand monks and lay disciples had long been waiting in the mountains. I stayed three weeks, and each night at the small assembly they heard the Dharma, each one full of joy, as I set forth the secret practices of Master Lianchi's whole life
(which shows how deeply Master Hanshan knew Master Lianchi)
. When the disciples heard this, some even wept, saying that I had brought forth what people did not know
(thinking that all I recounted was what the many did not know)
, and they asked me to compose a stupa inscription
(the Stupa Inscription for Master Yunqi Lianchi Hong)
The “Stupa Inscription for Master Yunqi Lianchi Hong” composed by Master Hanshan is deeply moving; see in detail
the Stupa Inscription for Master Lianchi

blocks.text: 5. Reciting the Buddha and Copying the Sutra

inline.s: Master Hanshan, in the Collection of Dream Wanderings
in his Autobiographical Chronological Account, says:
In the fifth year
(the fifth year of the Wanli era)
dingchou, when I was thirty-two. In the spring, returning from Yanmen, I reflected that the boundless
(without limit)

kindness of my parents could not be repaid, and that my course in the Dharma had many obstacles. Because I saw the vow-text of Master Si of Nanyue, I resolved to pierce myself and write a copy of the Avatamsaka Sutra in blood-ground gold — above, to form the excellent condition with prajna; below, to repay the boundless kindness — and I conceived the plan in the spring of that year. Formerly, the Holy Mother Cishang
(the Empress Dowager Li Cishang, natural mother of the Ming Shenzong emperor, who believed in Buddhism most fervently and gave alms most widely, so that the capital called her the Buddhist dame)
to protect the state chose monks to recite sutras, and I presumptuously
jiàn
, a self-deprecating expression)
had my name entered. When I arrived there
(having arrived there)
, the Empress Dowager heard of my writing the sutra
(the Empress Dowager had heard that I was going to
pierce myself and write the Avatamsaka Sutra in blood-ground gold
, and at once bestowed gold and paper to assist me. In April of the next year the writing of the sutra began
(the copying of the sutra began)

[Piercing oneself to write a copy of the Avatamsaka Sutra in blood-ground gold] Piercing the tongue to draw fresh blood, mixed with gold dust, to copy a single Avatamsaka Sutra. Master Yinguang says: “Master Hanshan's writing of the sutra was only because the Empress Dowager supplied him with paper and gold. The paper for gold-letter writing must be blue to make it show; on white paper it would not show.
So Hanshan, at the Miaode Hermitage on Mount Wutai, pierced his tongue, mixed the blood with gold, and wrote the Avatamsaka Sutra.” (From the Collected Prose of Master Yinguang
Letter One in Reply to Master Hongyi)
In the sixth year
(the sixth year of the Wanli era)
wuyin, when I was thirty-three. With fixed resolve
(with concentrated single-mindedness)
I wrote the sutra; whether the dot or stroke was large or small, at every fall of the brush I recited the Buddha's name.”
Master Hanshan, in the Collection of Dream Wanderings
in his “Letter to the Chan Practitioner Xingchu on Copying the Sutra,” says:
The old man
(Master Hanshan referring to himself)

once dwelt at Mount Wutai, and pierced himself to write the great Avatamsaka Sutra in blood-ground gold. Whenever I was writing, regardless of the dot or stroke of the character, whether large or small, long or short, as soon as I laid down one stroke I recited the Buddha's name. Thus, dot by dot and stroke by stroke, the light of the mind overflowed, thought after thought never interrupted, never forgotten, never wrong, never missed. After a long time, it made no difference whether I wrote or did not write; even in sleep it all became one mass. Thereupon, in all realms, whether active and confused or clamorous and noisy, the mind was perfectly still, and I attained the door of liberation wherein all realms are free and unobstructed; even all that I saw and heard was nothing but the true sutra manifest before me.”

Master Hanshan often instructed students in reciting the Buddha's name, and such instruction is found everywhere in the Collection of Dream Wanderings. Especially in the “Reply to the Questions of Prince De” in the Collection of Dream Wanderings
he gives, on how to recite the Buddha's name, an instruction of particular penetration; I now excerpt and annotate it as follows:

Throughout the six periods of the day, simply place the one sound “Amitabha Buddha” across your breast: never forget it in thought, never dim it in mind. Put aside all worldly affairs and think of them no more; take only this one phrase of the Buddha as the root of your own life. Grit your teeth and resolve never to let it go, so that even in eating and drinking, rising and resting, walking, standing, sitting and lying, this one sound of the Buddha is ever present before you.

The Buddha-name is the very root of life for putting an end to birth and death and escaping the cycle; it must never be left, even for an instant — walking, standing, sitting and lying, this one sound of the Buddha-name should be ever present.
This is to say: first, attain an unbroken recitation of the Buddha.
If you encounter states of adversity or prosperity, joy or anger, affliction or vexation, and the mind is ill at ease, then lift up this
(this)
one sound of the Buddha with a sharp squeeze, and you will see the affliction vanish that very moment. For thinking thought after thought of affliction
(using thought to dwell upon affliction)
is the bitter root of birth and death; now, by reciting the Buddha to dissolve affliction
(now by using the thought of the Buddha to dissolve affliction)
, that is the very means by which the Buddha ferries across the bitter place of birth and death
(that is the very means by which Amitabha Buddha ferries sentient beings across the bitter place of birth and death)
. If reciting the Buddha can dissolve affliction, then you can settle birth and death — there is no other method.

What your thoughts are determines your next life. Thinking of affliction leads into the cycle of birth and death; reciting the Buddha leads out of the cycle of birth and death. Remember this above all: “If reciting the Buddha can dissolve affliction, then you can settle birth and death — there is no other method.”
The word za
zǎn
means to squeeze and press.
Second, attain a recitation of the Buddha that dissolves affliction.

If your recitation of the Buddha becomes master even in the midst of affliction, then you will be master even in sleep and dreams; if you are master in sleep and dreams, then you will be master even in sickness and pain; if you are master in sickness and pain, then at the moment of death you will know clearly and distinctly where you are going.
Then, reciting the Buddha until you are master over affliction, master over sleep and dreams, and master over sickness and pain.

This matter is not hard to practice. One need only fix a single thought upon the urgency of birth and death, and single-mindedly rely upon one recitation of the Buddha, never again turning toward any other thinking. When this has long grown pure and familiar, one will naturally attain great peace and ease, great joy and benefit, utterly beyond the pleasures of the five worldly desires.

When the resolve to end birth and death is urgent, naturally nothing remains difficult. The key is to practice it gradually and uphold it persistently; where utmost sincerity is reached, even metal and stone give way.

(The five desires) Form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. Form is beautiful appearance; sound is melodious voice; smell is fragrant odor; taste is delicious flavor; touch is agreeable sensation. Because these five can give rise to a mind of greed and desire, they are called the five desires.

blocks.text: 7. Reciting the Buddha and Practicing Chan

inline.s: For a long time the two schools of Chan and Pure Land had argued without reaching agreement, as incompatible as fire and water. Master Hanshan, standing from a higher vantage, united Chan and Pure Land: reciting the Buddha is itself practicing Chan. Master Hanshan instructed:
If we speak of the mind-only Pure Land
(that is, if we speak of the Pure Land as mind-only)

, then one whose mind is pure attains a pure land. Therefore, when one first investigates Chan and has not yet awakened, without reciting the Buddha there is no way to purify one’s own mind — yet when the mind is pure, one awakens to the mind. Having awakened, the bodhisattva does not forsake Buddha-recitation; thus, without reciting the Buddha there is no way to attain perfect enlightenment. How do we know that all the patriarchs did not awaken to the mind through reciting the Buddha? If one recites until the mind is single and unconfused, afflictions are dissolved and one clearly understands one’s own mind — this is called awakening. If so, reciting the Buddha is itself practicing Chan. If one is like a bodhisattva, then this is not forsaking Buddha-recitation after awakening. Therefore all the patriarchs of old never forsook the Pure Land. Thus, reciting the Buddha is practicing Chan, and practicing Chan is to be reborn in the Pure Land.”
(The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions to the Chan Practitioner Huijing.)

(Reciting the Buddha is practicing Chan) Practicing Chan is to purify the mind so as to awaken to the mind. The passage above says: “When one first investigates Chan and has not yet awakened, without reciting the Buddha there is no way to purify one’s own mind.” “If one recites until the mind is single and unconfused, afflictions are dissolved and one clearly understands one’s own mind — this is called awakening. If so, reciting the Buddha is itself practicing Chan.” “How do we know that all the patriarchs did not awaken to the mind through reciting the Buddha?” Therefore reciting the Buddha is practicing Chan. Moreover, the supreme advantage of practicing Chan in this way is that it is not necessary to exhaust all afflictions before ending birth and death. Hence Buddha-recitation is a definitive Dharma-gate that encompasses the three faculties, rounds up both sudden and gradual paths, and is accomplished within a single lifetime.

Reciting the Buddha is practicing Chan; there are no other two methods. While reciting the Buddha, one must first set down all the afflictions, false thoughts, greed, hatred, and delusion, and all the myriad confused thoughts within one’s breast. Set them down to the point where there is nothing left to set down, then simply lift up the single recitation “Amitabha Buddha,” distinctly and clearly, so that it continues without interruption in the mind, like a thread strung with pearls. Again, it is like arrow-nocks joined end to end, with not the slightest gap between them. Exerting oneself to rest upon it in this way, one is not swept away by conditions of the environment in any situation. Using the mind like this day by day, in activity one is neither mixed nor confused, sleeping and waking are as one. Using the mind like this, when one recites until the moment of death the mind is single and unconfused — then that is the very time of transcending birth and death and of rebirth in the Pure Land.”
(The Dream-Wandering Collection
Instructions to the Chan Practitioner Ningxu.)

(Not interrupted in the mind) The mind’s recollection continuing without break. (Arrow-nocks joined end to end) Arrows joined one after another, head joined to tail. Kuò, the nock at the end of an arrow.

This Dharma-gate requires first, a resolve that is determined; second, being able to let go; third, being able to accord with conditions — and to accord with conditions is to be content with one’s lot; fourth, recognizing truly — that is, without delusion; fifth, detesting suffering deeply — since when the mind of detesting suffering is urgent, desire naturally departs and one does not fall away. With these five essentials, simply uphold the single thought.”

(Translation: This Dharma-gate requires first, a resolve that is determined; second, being able to let go; third, being able to accord with conditions, and to accord with conditions is to be content with one’s lot; fourth, recognizing truly, and recognizing truly is to be without delusion; fifth, detesting suffering deeply, and since the mind of detesting suffering is urgent, desire naturally departs and one does not fall away. With these five essentials, simply uphold the single thought.) (
The Dream-Wandering Collection
Letter to the Military Officer Chen Jiannan.)

blocks.text: 8. Diligent Practice of the Pure Karma

inline.s: Master Hanshan himself practiced in person, reciting the Buddha and being reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. In a letter from his later years, the master wrote:
And fearing that my remaining days are few, and that birth and death are urgent, I have closed the door, severed all connections, and simply lift up the single thought, awaiting only death
(for the rest of this life)
. Yesterday, on the Mid-Autumn Festival, I had already begun this
(yesterday, on the Mid-Autumn Festival, I had already begun to shut the door, sever all connections, and lift up a single Buddha-name)

. For more than twenty years I have recited; amid the wind and waves of the sea of suffering, the green mountains and white clouds have often come to me in dreams. Now that at last I have attained this, how could I regard it as an ordinary matter? In my present retreat
(within closed seclusion)
I have laid aside all the doctrines of Chan and the Dharma, and cling only to plain simplicity
(simply single-mindedly reciting the Buddha; “plain simplicity” here means no longer investigating Chan or studying the teachings)

. I often recall the ancient ones reciting Amitabha a hundred thousand times day and night. Now, ashamed of my age and weakness, whose strength fails, I have tested myself and can commonly do a little more than half. I especially emulate Master Huiyuan
(Master Huiyuan)
the six watches of the Lotus Clepsydra
(the “Lotus Clepsydra” is a water-clock made of lotus by Huiyao, a disciple of Master Huiyuan, the founding teacher of the Pure Land school, used to mark time at the Lushan practice center)
, using incense in place of the flower-lotus
(I use burning incense to mark time in place of the Lotus Clepsydra)
. For several months past, body and mind have of themselves reached utmost bliss. Knowing that your concern for me is deep
(knowing that you are very concerned about me)
, I venture to tell you
(so I take the liberty of informing you)
(The Dream-Wandering Collection
Reply to the Historiographer Qian Shouzhi.)
Please note the phrase “for several months past, body and mind have of themselves reached utmost bliss” — this is a portrait of the state of the master’s Buddha-recitation in his later years.

blocks.text: 9. Directing All to the Pure Land

inline.s: Master Hanshan not only recited the Buddha himself and sought rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, but also strongly maintained that all Dharma-gates should be directed to the Pure Land.
(Master Hanshan not only recited the Buddha himself and sought rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss) Master Hanshan, in the third year of the Tianqi reign (
), passed into stillness on the thirteenth day of the tenth month, at the age of seventy-eight. According to the Chronicle of Master Hanshan:
“At noon
the thirteenth day of the tenth month
at noon)
, after Mr. Zhang
(the prefect of Shaoyang, Zhang Sanxing, entered the mountain to present purple silk and a monastic robe to congratulate the master on his birthday;
the twelfth day of the tenth month
was the master’s birthday)

had taken his leave, the master called for the attendant to bring pure water to rinse his mouth, and said: “Today I cut off the trailing vine.” He then asked for hot water to bathe and change his clothes,
while the assembly surrounded him reciting the Buddha
. He instructed them: “Do not be alarmed; you should follow the Buddha’s rule, do not don coarse mourning, do not weep,
single-mindedly recite the Buddha
.” At the shen hour
(three o’clock in the afternoon)

, the master sat upright and passed away. That night a ray of light illumined the heavens, the flocks of birds cried mournfully, monks and layfolk grieved and wailed, the sound shaking the mountain valleys. After his passing, he sat upright for three days, his face pale and fair with ruddy lips, his hands and feet soft and pliant, as if in samādhi.”
This shows that Master Hanshan was reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
In the Preface Directing the Mind to the Pure Land of the Dream-Wandering Collection

, the master wrote: “As for the gate of the Pure Land, it universally covers the three faculties; both sudden and gradual enter together, and no capacity is excluded. This is what is called transcending the three realms horizontally — it is the supreme Dharma-gate. Among all the patriarchs of old and the wise ones who awakened to mind, there is not one who did not take this as their final home; Nāgārjuna (Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna) and Aśvaghosa (Bodhisattva Aśvaghosa) praised it with all their might.” “Those of the most superior faculty in Chan have never failed to return to the Pure Land.” I now extract and annotate this passage as follows:

“Directing to the Pure Land means directing the practitioner home to the Pure Land. Our world-honored Buddha, in gathering and transforming sentient beings, set forth Dharma-gates whose skillful means were many and various. The essential teachings from beginning to end comprise the two schools of nature and form. Because the capacities of beings differ in size, therefore the teaching are established as sudden and gradual. In the end they divide into the two gates of Chan and teaching: the teaching gate draws in the three faculties, while the Chan gate suddenly enlightens the one mind. The whole of the great canon and the seventeen hundred case studies have come down from long ago.”

“Directing to the Pure Land” means guiding the practitioner to return to the Pure Land. Our world-honored Buddha, gathering and transforming sentient beings, taught according to capacity and set forth Dharma-gates of many kinds. The essential teachings from beginning to end comprise the Dharma-Nature school and the Dharma-Form school. This is because the faculties of sentient beings differ in size, so the teaching gate is established as sudden and gradual. In the end it divides into the two gates of Chan and teaching. The teaching gate draws in the three faculties (the supreme, the middling, and the inferior), while the Chan gate suddenly enlightens the one mind. Like the whole of the great canon and the seventeen hundred case studies, from long ago they have always drawn in the three faculties and suddenly enlightened the one mind.

(The two schools of nature and form) The Dharma-Nature school (Nature school for short) and the Dharma-Form school (Form school for short). (The one mind) A name for the original nature, the Buddha-nature, the Tathāgatagarbha. Master Hanshan’s Record of the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra says: “Deluded, the one mind becomes the eight consciousnesses.” It also says: “The still and extinct is called the one mind; the one mind is called the Tathāgatagarbha.” This means: the Tathāgatagarbha (original nature) deluded turns into the storehouse consciousness (habitual nature), giving rise to the eight consciousnesses — Ālaya, manas, mind-consciousness, eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness. The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra says: “The self means the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha. All sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature — that is my meaning. Such a self as this, from the beginning, has always been covered by measureless afflictions, and therefore sentient beings cannot see it.” It also says: “What the Tathāgata now speaks of as the true self is called the Buddha-nature.”

“As for the gate of the Pure Land, it universally covers the three faculties; both sudden and gradual enter together, and no capacity is excluded. What is called transcending the three realms horizontally is the supreme Dharma-gate. Among all the patriarchs of old and the wise ones who awakened to mind, there is not one who did not take this as their final home; Nāgārjuna and Aśvaghosa praised it with all their might.”

As for this gate of the Pure Land, it universally covers the three faculties; both sudden and gradual enter together, and no capacity is excluded. What is called transcending the three realms horizontally is the supreme Dharma-gate. Among all the patriarchs of old and the wise ones who awakened to the one mind, there is not one who did not take this as their final home; for example, Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna and Bodhisattva Aśvaghosa both praised it with all their might.

(Transcending the three realms horizontally) The Pure Land Dharma-gate transcends the three realms horizontally and so ends birth and death; other Dharma-gates transcend the three realms vertically (having exhausted all afflictions) and so end birth and death. Master Yinguang says: “If one speaks of the vertical transcendence, without strenuously cultivating the Way of precepts, meditation, and wisdom and exhausting all affliction and confusion it cannot be done. If the afflictions and confusion have not been entirely exhausted, then one still cannot leave the three realms. Moreover, sentient beings of the last age have shallow roots of goodness and short lives; among cultivators, even if there are a hundred million, those who transcend are hardly one in several. Because they rely solely on their own power, it is difficult to gain actual benefit. If one speaks of the horizontal transcendence, one need only rely on the Pure Land Dharma-gate, give rise to faith and make a vow, recite the Buddha-name and seek rebirth in the West. Together with this, be earnest in the relations of human duty, fulfill one’s own part to the full, do no evil and practice all good, then not one in ten thousand is lost, and all gain rebirth. Having been reborn there, one ends birth and death, transcends the ordinary and enters the holy, forever departs from all suffering, and enjoys only all bliss. Those whose practice is mature surely reach the highest grade; and those who merely recite at the point of death also join the lowest grade. This relies entirely on the Buddha’s power, and its benefit is as far apart from that of those relying solely on their own power as heaven from earth.”
Preface on the Rise of the Lotus Society of Horizontal Transcendence)

“Those who say it is only to lift up the middling and inferior do not understand the purport of the Pure Land. Why? Because the retribution of body (primary) and environment (secondary) of all sentient beings in the ten directions, though having differences of superior and inferior, pure and defiled, all arise from the transforming functions of the one mind. Therefore it is said, ‘when the mind is pure, the land is pure’ — this is what is called the mind-only Pure Land. Thus the land is not outside the mind; its purity comes from the one mind. If one is not a wise one who has awakened to mind, how can one purify that land? This is why those of the most superior faculty in Chan have never failed to return to the Pure Land.”

Those who discuss it and suppose that the Pure Land Dharma-gate is merely for the sake of uplifting the middling and inferior faculties have not understood the purport of the Pure Land. Why? Because the retribution of body (the environment and the body-and-mind) of all sentient beings in the ten directions, though having differences of superior and inferior, pure and defiled, all arise from the transforming functions of the one mind. When the mind is pure, it transforms into the superior and pure secondary and primary retributions; when the mind is defiled, it transforms into the inferior and defiled secondary and primary retributions. Therefore it is said, “when the mind is pure, the land is pure” — this is what is called the mind-only Pure Land. Thus the land is not outside the mind; the purity of the land comes entirely from the purity of the one mind. If one is not a wise one who has awakened to the one mind, how can one purify that land? Therefore those of the most superior faculty in Chan have never failed to return to the Pure Land — this is the reason.

(Primary and secondary retribution) Primary retribution refers to the body-and-mind of sentient beings, which is the proper result brought about by karmic causes of the past, and so is called primary retribution. Secondary retribution is the environment in which the body-and-mind (primary retribution) dwells, which is also a result brought about by past karmic causes — such as lands, mountains, rivers, the earth, houses, and implements.

“Those of the middling and inferior faculties, practicing pure precepts and concentrating single-mindedly in contemplation, with thought and contemplation continuing in succession, will surely gain rebirth at the end of life. Though there is the appearance of going and coming, yet the marks of Amitabha’s excellent appearance, the jeweled trees, the flower thrones, are truly manifested by one’s own mind — like a dream, they do not come from outside. As for the simple and ignorant men and women who merely practice the ten good deeds, strictly uphold the five precepts, and single-mindedly recite the Buddha, they will surely gain rebirth at death: this is because the Buddha’s power upholds them and the practitioner’s recollection grows ever stronger. With this excellent thought on the one side and the Buddha’s great vow on the other, the vow and the thought connect, and one’s own mind and the Buddha silently respond to each other. Although the state of the Pure Land has not yet appeared, the merit of rebirth is already accomplished — truly brought about by the power of one’s own mind’s subtle response, and not from outside either. If those who have committed the ten evils, with karma strong at the end of life, and the sufferings of hell already appearing before them, are pressed to the extreme by suffering and their wish to escape is urgent, then this extreme suffering becomes the power of thought, and they bring their remorse to the utmost, and when remorse has reached its utmost, at this very extreme a complete transformation occurs and a single thought responds to the Buddha. So the Buddha’s power upholds them and appears before the thought, turning the mountain of swords into jeweled trees and the cauldron of fire into a lotus pond — hence even these evil ones gain rebirth. Yet this state of the Pure Land indeed comes from the power of the complete transformation of one’s own mind; truly it is not gained from outside.”

Those of the middling and inferior faculties, practicing pure precepts and concentrating single-mindedly, with contemplation and thought continuing in succession, will surely gain rebirth at the end of life. Though there is the appearance of going and coming, yet the marks of Amitabha’s excellent appearance, the jeweled trees, and the flower thrones are truly manifested by one’s own mind — like a dream, they do not come from outside. As for the simple and ignorant men and women who merely practice the ten good deeds, strictly uphold the five precepts, and single-mindedly recite the Buddha, they will surely gain rebirth at death: this is because the Buddha’s power upholds them and the practitioner’s recollection grows ever stronger. The practitioner with this excellent thought, and Amitabha with his great vow — the vow and the thought connect, and one’s own mind and the Buddha silently respond to each other. Although the state of the Pure Land has not yet appeared, the merit of rebirth is already accomplished — truly brought about by the power of one’s own mind’s subtle response, and not from outside either. If those who have committed the ten evils, with karma strong at the end of life, and the sufferings of hell already appearing before them, are pressed to the extreme by suffering and their wish to escape is urgent, then this extreme suffering becomes the power of thought, and they bring their remorse to the utmost; and when remorse has reached its utmost, at this very extreme a complete transformation occurs and a single thought responds to the Buddha. So the Buddha’s power upholds them and appears before the thought, turning the mountain of swords of hell into the jeweled trees of the Land of Bliss and the cauldron of fire of hell into its lotus pond — hence even these evil ones gain rebirth. Yet this state of the Pure Land indeed comes from the power of the complete transformation of one’s own mind; truly it is not gained from outside.

“Looking at it from this, there is not a single dharma among the myriad dharmas of the three realms that does not arise from the mind; and there is not a single state, pure or defiled, that is not manifested from the mind. Therefore in the single gate of the Pure Land, whether one is awakened or not, whether of superior intelligence or inferior dullness, the reason that all who cultivate inevitably attain it is that it is all from one’s own mind. This being so, the purport of the mind-only Pure Land is as clear as seeing black and white. Because the Buddha-body is like emptiness and one’s own mind is empty and pure, in mysterious unity with the Buddha, merely borrowing the adornment of a single thought of vow-power, the state of the Pure Land suddenly appears without relying on merit or rank — this is the supreme, utterly beyond the reach of shallow wisdom and meager faith.”

Looking at it from this, there is not a single dharma among the myriad dharmas of the three realms that is not the transforming function of the mind; and there is not a single state, pure or defiled, that is not manifested from the mind. Therefore in the single gate of the Pure Land, whether one is awakened or not, whether of superior intelligence or inferior dullness, the reason that all who cultivate inevitably attain it is that it is all from one’s own mind. This being so, the purport of the mind-only Pure Land is as clear as seeing black and white. Because the Buddha-body is like emptiness, and the practitioner’s own mind is empty and pure, in mysterious unity with the Buddha, merely borrowing the adornment of a single thought of vow-power, the state of the Pure Land suddenly appears without relying on merit or rank — this is the supreme Dharma-gate, utterly beyond the comprehension of the shallow-witted and thin in faith.

(Mysterious unity) The state of being merged and indistinguishable, with no distinction of self and other, is called mysterious unity. (Merit and rank) A Chan institution term, referring to the fruits of practice and the stages of attainment.

“Those of the middling and inferior faculties, relying on thought and contemplation continuing in succession, are not toppled by the objects of love or the karmic habits. Their faculties, though somewhat inferior, are in aspiration truly superior; and their cultivation is difficult because cutting off the root of love is hard. Rebirth for the evil is even more difficult. Though it is said they carry their karma, it is also produced by the internal influence of the roots of goodness of many past lives. Their faculties, though base and evil, yet with a single mind of heroic vigor surpass the most superior. Compared to those who put down the butcher’s knife and at once do Buddha-work, they are even a step superior. Yet that such evil ones gain rebirth at death is not one in ten thousand; if people of the world must wait for this to seek rebirth, they are utterly mistaken. As I see it, the faculties have no difference of great or small; in the end one must accomplish it by the single upward thought. So this Dharma-gate — how could it be established only for the sake of the middling and inferior?”

Those of the middling and inferior faculties, relying on thought and contemplation continuing in succession, are not toppled by the objects of love or the karmic habits. Their faculties, though somewhat inferior, are in aspiration truly superior; and their cultivation is difficult because cutting off the root of love is hard. Rebirth for evil ones is even more difficult. Though it is said they carry their karma, it is also produced by the internal influence of the roots of goodness of many past lives. Their faculties, though base and evil, yet with a single mind of heroic vigor surpass the most superior. Compared to those who put down the butcher’s knife and at once do Buddha-work, they are even a step superior. Yet that such evil ones gain rebirth at death is not one in a hundred thousand; if people of the world must wait for this before seeking rebirth, they are utterly and greatly mistaken. As I see it, the faculties have no difference of great or small; in the end one must accomplish it by the single upward thought (turning from delusion to awakening). So this Dharma-gate — how could it be established only for the sake of those of middling and inferior faculties?

(Root of love) The afflictions of craving and desire forming the root that gives rise to other afflictions is called the root of love. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Samsara has love as its root.” (The single upward thought) A thought of the mind turning from delusion to awakening.
In the section “Instructions to the Pure Practitioner Xiyin” of the Dream-Wandering Collection
, Master Hanshan says:

“The world knows only that among the patriarchs’ heirs, awakening is supreme. The original intent of awakening to mind is to escape birth and death — is reciting the Buddha not a method of escaping birth and death? Many of those who investigate Chan do not necessarily escape, while those who recite the Buddha doubtlessly escape. The reason is that Chan requires the abandonment of thought, while Buddha-recitation is focused on thought. Because
(because)

sentient beings have long sunk in false thought, so to leave it is truly difficult. If one turns the defiled thought into a pure thought, this is to fight poison with poison, a method of exchange and replacement. Therefore, investigating is hard to awaken to, while Buddha-recitation is easy to accomplish. If one is truly urgent about birth and death, and recites the Buddha with the mind one uses to investigate, how could one worry about not ending birth and death within a single lifetime?”

The world knows only that among the patriarchs’ heirs, awakening to mind is supreme. Yet the original intent of awakening to mind is to escape birth and death — is reciting the Buddha not a method of escaping birth and death? Many of those who investigate Chan cannot necessarily escape, while those who recite the Buddha doubtlessly escape. The reason is that Chan requires the abandonment of thought, while Buddha-recitation lies in focusing the thought. Because sentient beings have long sunk in false thought from the beginningless eons, completely abandoning false thoughts is truly difficult. If one turns the defiled thought into a pure thought, this is to fight poison with poison, using the Buddha-name to replace false thoughts — a method of exchange and replacement, and therefore easy. So investigating is hard to awaken to, while Buddha-recitation is easy to accomplish. If one is truly urgent about birth and death, and recites the Buddha with the mind one uses to investigate, how could one worry about not ending birth and death within a single lifetime?

Master Hanshan’s life of practice began with Buddha-recitation and ended with Buddha-recitation, taking “various auspicious signs as the evidence of rebirth.” (The twelfth-generation patriarch of the Pure Land school, Master Chewu, said: “Various auspicious signs serve as evidence of rebirth.” See the Collected Works of Master Chewu.)
The Praise of Portraits of the Eighty-Eight Patriarchs records of Master Hanshan: “

In the dingsi year he returned to Mount Lu and built the Fayun Temple beneath Wuru Peak, emulating Master Huiyuan’s clepsydra of six watches and applying himself solely to the Pure karma. In the renxu year of the Tianqi reign he again resided at Caoxi. In the guihai year, on the eleventh day of the tenth month, he manifested a slight illness, bathed and burned incense, gathered the assembly, and took leave. He looked at them and said: Today I cut off the trailing vine. He sat upright and passed away. He was seventy-eight years old, with sixty years of monkhood. ... Earlier, in the yichou year, the coffin was returned to the Fayun Temple pagoda beneath Wuru Peak on Mount Lu and enshrined. In the guiwei year of the Chongzhen reign, people of Guangdong again conveyed his coffin back to Caoxi. Twenty years having passed, he sat upright as if alive; so they applied gold paint to the body, enshrined it on a dais, facing the mummy of the Sixth Patriarch, and set up a place of offering at the old pagoda courtyard on Tianqi Ridge, naming it Hanshan Courtyard, half a ‘li’ from Nanhua Temple.”

(Trailing vine) A Chan institution term. It means that written words and speech, spreading and interweaving like a vine, were used to explain and illustrate principle, but instead entangle and bind one. To make idle talk, to chatter about trifles, is called “pulling the trailing vine.”
(Twenty years having passed, he sat upright as if alive, so they applied gold paint to the body and enshrined him on a dais)

After Master Hanshan passed into stillness, his face was still as pure and lustrous as jade, his lips still so rosy, his hands and feet still so soft, just as when he was ordinarily in samādhi. The disciples escorted the master’s body to Mount Lu; and because the climate there was damp, the attendant Fushan built a pagoda court and placed the master’s body on the pagoda. Twenty years later, his Lingnan disciples went to Mount Lu to welcome the master back to Caoxi. When they reached Caoxi, the disciples guarding the coffin, Guangcheng and Cili, saw that the coffin had a crack
(a fissure), and so privately bored a small
hole to look within
, and saw the master’s body sitting upright as if alive,
and so they informed the assembly.
Opening the coffin chamber, they saw the master seated cross-legged in full lotus, as solemn as in life, with nails and hair still growing and his complexion still
ruddy

; the purple silk robe and the necklace of beads were still as new. Just then a gust of wind arose, and the clothing suddenly scattered like clouds breaking into stars, dancing in the wind; the people of the region gathered them up as auspicious symbols. At this moment a monk suddenly came forward, requesting to use the Indian method of keeping
the body intact,
in order to protect the master’s body.

After obtaining the assembly’s consent, he used sandalwood powder from Hainan, rubbing it over the master’s body so that it looked as if it were coated with a layer of lacquer. Having finished, the monk left on his own. While the master was alive, a devout laywoman of Caoxi had made a vow to embroider a robe of a thousand Buddhas to offer to the master; fearing her breath was impure, she wrapped her mouth in yellow silk while embroidering
When the robe of a thousand Buddhas was finished, the master had already
passed into stillness

and been placed in the coffin, and the robe was stored in a chest at the Baolin treasury. Now the robe was brought out and draped on the master’s body, and though twenty years had passed, it shone brilliantly as if newly made. After the sealing of the coffin was completed, the disciples laid the master to rest at the old pagoda courtyard, renaming it Hanshan Temple, about half a ‘li’ from Nanhua Temple where the Sixth Patriarch’s body rests. Following the custom of the offerings to the Sixth Patriarch, every morning the disciples bathed the master’s face with a bowl of hot fragrant water to make it sweat, then wiped it dry with a towel, and just as when he was alive, offered food and drink. Once a year they also gave him a bath. (Excerpted from The Life of Master Hanshan.)
Master Yinguang said: “Hanshan’s former vow was not yet fulfilled, therefore he again manifested birth as Jieliu
(Master Xingce)
. He reproved those who cultivate merely for human and heavenly blessings, calling them no better than icchantikas and caṇḍālas
(simply a class of icchantikas and caṇḍālas)

. The Buddha and my mind-nature are originally no different; the Buddha is already accomplished while I have not yet cultivated. If one wishes mind and Buddha to be without difference, one should seek it through recollecting the Buddha and reciting the Buddha.”
(The Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, the Tenth Patriarch of the Qing, Master Xingce of the Puren Temple on Yushan.)

(Icchantika) A short form of the one who has cut off all roots of goodness — one who does not believe in cause and effect, commits the five rebellious deeds and the ten evils, cuts off all roots of goodness, and falls into the AvÄ«ci hell. (Caṇḍāla) A short form of caṇḍāla, referring here to an evil person.
Master Xingce
, the tenth-generation patriarch of the Pure Land school)
, a native of Yixing, Jiangsu, whose lay surname was Jiang and whose style name was Jieliu. His father Quanchang was versed in both Confucianism and Buddhism, and was a close friend of Hanshan Deqing
(a close and dear friend of Master Hanshan)
. Five years after Deqing passed away, Quanchang dreamed that he entered his chamber carrying a staff, and Xingce was born
(Quanchang dreamed that Master Hanshan entered the chamber with a staff, and Xingce was born)

; therefore he named the boy Menghan (“Dream of Hanshan”). When he grew up and both parents died one after another, he resolved to leave the world. At the age of twenty-three, he went to the Li’an Temple in Wulin and left the household life under Master Wen of the Ruo
(ruò)
Hermitage. For five years he never let his side touch the mat
(he sat long without lying down)

, and suddenly penetrated the true source of the Dharma. After Master Wen passed away, the master lived at the Baoen Temple. There he met a fellow practitioner, Master Xi’an Ying, who urged him to cultivate the Pure karma. He also met Master Qiaoshi of Qiantang, who guided him to study the Tiantai teachings, and so together they entered a pure room and cultivated the samādhi of the Lotus Sutra. His past wisdom suddenly became clear, and he thoroughly fathomed the marrow of the teaching. In the second year of the Kangxi reign, he built a hermitage among the streams and islets of Xixi by Mount Fayuan in Hangzhou, applying himself solely to the Pure karma, and so named his dwelling the Lianzao Hermitage
fū
, the calyx of a flower)
. In the ninth year, he resided at the Puren Temple in Yushan and promoted the founding of a Lotus Society, and scholars eagerly
(xī)
followed him as their teacher
(scholars unanimously praised him and followed him)
He once
wrote the Essay Exhorting True Faith, saying:
The Buddha-recitation samādhi has come down from long ago
(its origin is of long standing)
. Though it is said to be of lofty merit and easy to advance, yet among practitioners of the last age, few obtain spiritual efficacy, truly because
(it is all because)
their faith and vow are not single-minded, so that they cannot guide their good conduct toward the essential end of rebirth in the Pure Land
(because they have not made rebirth in the Pure Land their essential aim)

(Guiding conduct with faith and vow) Using faith and vow to guide practice, and settling it upon practice. (Making rebirth in the Pure Land the essential aim) For a reciter of the Buddha, rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss should be regarded as the foremost great matter.

Now that we have widely invited good companions to cultivate together the pure karmic cause, unless we carefully examine the resolve of the mind, how do we know the essential path that escapes suffering? All of us who join this Dharma assembly must possess true faith. Without true faith, though one recite the Buddha and observe the fasts, release life and cultivate merit, one is but a good person of the world who is reborn in a good place to enjoy bliss. While enjoying that bliss, one again creates karma; and having created karma, one must fall into suffering. Viewed with the true eye, such a person is only one step short of the icchantikas and caṇḍālas. Is such faith true faith? What is called true faith

First, one must believe that mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are without difference in the three respects. I am the Buddha yet unaccomplished; Amitabha is the Buddha already accomplished; the nature of awakening is without a second. Though I am muddled and inverted, the nature of awakening has never been lost. Though I have turned through the eons, the nature of awakening has never moved. Therefore it is said, “the single thought turning back its light, one finds what was originally attained.”

Second, one must believe that I am the Buddha in principle and the Buddha in name, while Amitabha is the Buddha in ultimate realization. Though the nature is not two, the stages are as far apart as heaven from the deep. If I do not single-mindedly recollect that Buddha and seek rebirth in that land, I must surely follow karma and drift through transmigration, undergoing immeasurable suffering. This is what is meant by the dharma-body flowing through the five paths — it is not then called Buddha, but is called a sentient being.
(The Buddha in principle and the Buddha in name) The first two of the six stages of Buddhahood.

(The six stages of Buddhahood) The six stages marking the process by which an ordinary person cultivates up to Buddhahood: First, the Buddha in principle — though all sentient beings transmigrate in the six paths and dwell daily amidst the defilements and afflictions, turning their back on the essence of awakening, yet the merit of the Buddha-nature is still fully present; therefore it is called the “Buddha in principle.” Second, the Buddha in name — whether from a good teacher or from the scriptures, one hears of the Buddha-nature that is inherently present, unborn and unperishing, and understands it through words and names, suddenly awakening to it; therefore it is called the “Buddha in name.” Third, the Buddha in contemplation and practice — not merely understanding the words, one further cultivates contemplation according to the teaching, so that contemplation of the mind is clear and the wisdom corresponding to principle is united; therefore it is called the “Buddha in contemplation and practice.” (The wisdom corresponding to principle: principle is the realm contemplated, wisdom is the wisdom that contemplates; “corresponding” means matching, that the state and wisdom are commensurate and practice and words accord.) Fourth, the Buddha in resemblance — at this stage, in contemplation and practice the more one contemplates the clearer, the more one stills the more serene. Though one has not truly awakened and realized, yet in principle it is as if one had, like a true realization; therefore it is called the “Buddha in resemblance.” Fifth, the Buddha in partial realization — this is after the ten stages of faith, when one breaks through a portion of ignorance and realizes a portion of the three virtues, and enters the first abiding stage and realizes the dharma-body. From there one is a great dharma-body being; from the first abiding stage up to equal enlightenment, one passes through forty-one stages, each breaking through ignorance and realizing the three virtues, forty-one portions in all; therefore it is called the “Buddha in partial realization.” Sixth, the Buddha in ultimate realization — this is when, from equal enlightenment, one breaks through the final portion of ignorance, so that delusion is exhausted and truth is pure, the inherent true-nature Buddha-nature of this very body is fully realized, and one enters the stage of wondrous enlightenment to become a Buddha; therefore it is called the “Buddha in ultimate realization.”
(The three virtues)
First, the virtue of the dharma-body
second, the virtue of prajñā
third, the virtue of liberation.

Third, one must believe that though I am heavily veiled by obstacles and laden with heavy karma, having long dwelt in the realm of suffering, I am a sentient being within Amitabha’s mind. Though Amitabha, adorned with all virtues, is far away in a land beyond unthinkable billions of Buddha-realms, he is the Buddha within my own mind. Since the mind-nature is without a second, naturally there is the karmic confluence of response and response, like a magnet drawing iron — there is nothing to doubt. This is what is meant by recollecting the Buddha and reciting the Buddha, and without fail seeing the Buddha now and in the future, and not being far from the Buddha.
(The karmic confluence of response) The response of sentient beings and the response of Amitabha mutually interpenetrate.

One who possesses the above threefold true faith: though it be the merit of a hair and the blessing of a mote of dust, all can be dedicated to the Western Land and adorn the Pure Land. How much the more so with keeping a pure diet and upholding precepts, releasing life and giving charity, reciting the Mahāyāna scriptures, and making offerings to the Three Jewels — these manifold good deeds, are they not enough to fill the provisions for the Pure Land? It is only because their faith is not genuine that they sink into the outflows. Hence in practice today there is no other essential method: if within the six hours of the day and night one adds to oneself this threefold true faith, then in every act and course
(that is, every good deed one performs)
, one's effort is never cast away in vain.
the outflows (yǒu lòu)
