] Here it refers to the cause of the outflows: the karmic cause that brings the retribution of the three realms (the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm). [Cast away in vain (táng juān)] To be wasted and abandoned in vain.
Once he undertook a seven-day retreat of vigorous practice and composed a discourse to show to the assembly, saying:

The seven days of invoking the Name place value in having the mind single and unconfused, unbroken and unmingled; it is not necessarily that quick recitation and much recitation are superior. Only, neither slack nor hurried, reciting the Name close and close, so that the Buddha-name within the mind stands clear and distinct. In dressing and eating, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying, the single great name continues fine and unbroken, like one's breathing: neither scattered nor sunk. To recite the Name thus, one may be called one who is able to be single-minded and diligent in practice. If one is a true stream of the Way
(a stream of the Way, one who pursues the Way)
, one can at once investigate that all dharmas are Suchness
(“Suchness,” dharma-nature, and reality are all names for the true nature of all dharmas)

, without a second characteristic. That is to say, sentient beings and the Buddha are non-dual; self and other are non-dual; the subjective and the objective are non-dual; purity and defilement are non-dual; suffering and joy are non-dual; longing
(the same as “yearning”)

and aversion are non-dual; grasping and rejecting are non-dual; bodhi and affliction are non-dual; birth and death and nirvana are non-dual. All these pairs of dharmas are of a single characteristic, one pure path, needing no forced arrangement
(no deliberate arrangement)
; only investigate as it is
(one is simply to investigate as it is: all dharmas are Suchness, without a second characteristic)

. When investigation reaches its limit, it of a sudden agrees with one's own original mind. Then one knows that dressing and eating are always samādhi; that laughter, play, anger, and abuse are none other than Buddha-work; and that the distracted mind and the concentrated mind are in the end but empty talk. Throughout the six hours of day and night, one cannot find so much as a hair's breadth of difference; although one invokes the Name with a sincere mind
(the same as “recite”)

, it is the same as cursing at will; although one practices diligently, it is also ascetic toil within a dream. To be thus clearly penetrated — only then is one a true student of the Way, single-minded and diligent in invoking the Name.
The first single-mindedness
(single-mindedness in matters, one-pointed unconcern)
seems difficult yet is easy; the second single-mindedness
(single-mindedness in principle, one-pointed unconcern)

seems easy yet is hard. One who can attain only the first single-mindedness will surely attain rebirth. One who also attains the second can climb to the highest grade. Yet these two kinds of single-mindedness are both matters within the reach of ordinary beings on this plane
(they are the practices an ordinary being can do)
; whoever has a mind can study and practice them. Fellow monastics and laypeople in the same hall
(monks and laypeople)

, do not on any account revere the sage's realm too high and content yourselves with the lowly. Each must diligently urge on body and mind: in the near case, within these seven days; in the far case, throughout a lifetime. Always hold this faith, always practice this practice. Even if one does not attain the realization
(even if one does not realize the state of agreeing with one's own original mind)
, the cause is still a strong one, and the grade of transformation within the lotus palace
(the grade of the lotus-bud transformation)
, will surely not be among the middle or lower grades. If, however, after the seven days one turns a deaf ear, and the familiar place
(referring to emotional attachments)
after all does not arise, and the place where life is engendered
(referring to Buddha-recitation)

is still hard to make familiar; and ignorance and karmic habits, pulling and intertwining, and one merely wishes to claim the merit of seven days, while these seven days have not even reached the ground of single-minded unconcern — then this is precisely what is called having little good roots, virtue, and causes. How can one hope to be reborn in that land? Causing the words of truth from the golden mouth to be doubted as fraud — whose fault is this? Pure assembly of these seven days, may each of you examine himself and be admonished and encouraged.

[Matters within the reach of ordinary beings on this plane] The matters of the side of the ordinary being in this vast, benighted state. The ordinary being of the broad earth is also called the ordinary being of the thin ground, referring to the position of an ordinary being. [Thin ground] As for “thin,” it means “pressed upon.” The “thin ground” is the position in which one is pressed upon by all kinds of suffering — it refers to the realm of the ordinary being. The Contemplation of the Pure Mind on Precepts and Dharma says: “The ordinary being on the thin ground has a foul body and a lowly, contemptible constitution, and the retribution is base and mean.”

He dwelt at Pure Benevolence [temple] for thirteen years, and in the twenty-first year of the Kangxi reign, on the ninth day of the seventh month, he passed away at the age of fifty-five. At that time there was one Sun Han, who died of illness and revived after a full day and night. He said: I was seized by the underworld and bound before the King of Yama. In the darkness, of a sudden I beheld a light shining to the heavens, with fragrance and flowers filling the sky, and Yama prostrating on the ground, welcoming the Great Master who had gone West. I asked: What master is this? They said: Jieliu
(that is, Master Xingce)
. Because I was illuminated by the master's light, I was released. On the same day there was a son of the Wu family who died of illness and revived the following night
(the second night)
, and described in full what he had seen, just as Sun Han had said.

In praise: Master Hanshan, because his former vow was not yet fulfilled, returned to save beings and manifested as Master Jieliu. He promoted the Pure Land, urging people to rely on it single-mindedly with faith and vow to guide their practice, to practice vigorously in invoking the Name, and to understand the first principle. His discrimination of the teachings, and his rules for the seven-day single-minded vigorous recitation retreat and so forth, exhaust the understanding and practice of the Pure Land school, and are enough to serve as a ferry and bridge for later generations. His return to the West was honored by the underworld, an affair similar to Yongming
(a great monk of the Song dynasty, sixth patriarch of the Pure Land school)
. One may say the former patriarch and the latter patriarch — their standard
kuí
is one, indeed
(they are the same)

[The first principle] The supreme and unsurpassable truth, that is, the ultimate doctrine of the middle way — neither empty nor existent — of true emptiness and wondrous existence. [The discrimination of teachings] Master Jieliu authored a treatise, The Discrimination of the Dharma Door. [Discrimination (liào jiǎn)] also written as choosing and selecting; it means to pick and choose. The “discrimination” in scriptures and treatises often refers to the skillful distinguishing and choosing of the true Dharma. [Ferry and bridge] A crossing and a bridge. Here it is a metaphor for the method and the path by which one is ferried to liberation.
